results.title: Analyst Sees AI Compute Futures Boom - The New Boston
highlights:
AI compute could soon trade like oil or electricity, according to a new call from Silicon Data analyst Carmen Li, who says futures on compute may rival top commodity markets. Her view lands as demand for graphics chips and data center time surges and supply remains tight. Investors, cloud providers, and developers are all watching for new ways to price and hedge access to scarce compute capacity.

...

Over the past two years, developers have struggled to secure high-end chips and stable access to training clusters. Spot prices for rented GPUs have swung sharply. Cloud credits and long-term reservations offered some relief but left many buyers exposed to sudden shortages.

Commodity-style contracts could push the market beyond ad hoc deals. In oil and power, futures help smooth shocks and guide investment. A similar tool for compute could set clearer reference prices for model training runs and large inference deployments.

...

Exchanges or electronic platforms could list monthly or quarterly contracts. Buyers would post margin and settle daily, as they do in power and metals. Delivery could be physical access to a cluster or cash-settled against a public index of GPU-hour prices.

Li’s forecast rests on a few trends: expanding AI budgets, persistent supply constraints, and the need for planning tools. If producers can hedge multi-year output, they may finance new data centers more easily. If buyers can lock prices, they can plan model cycles without fear of a price spike.

...

Compute does not exist without electricity and cooling. Power prices vary by region and hour, and shortages can halt training jobs. Traders say any compute contract must account for local energy costs and grid constraints. That linkage could add volatility but also create hedging pairs with electricity futures.

Supply chains add another layer. Lead times for chips and networking gear remain long, which can make future delivery risky. A producer who sells too much forward could face penalties if hardware slips. Careful margining and position limits would be needed to avoid stress in a crunch.

results.title: ⚠️CHART OF THE WEEK: The AI gap between China and the US is quickly narrowing
highlights:
The price companies are paying for AI model usage has fallen to $1.67 per million tokens, the lowest level since mid April and down more than –20% from its May peak. 

 In simple terms, this measures how much businesses are paying for AI output, and it has now declined for 3 weeks. 

 This comes as cheaper and open-source AI models are becoming increasingly competitive. Recently, a combination of 3 mid-tier models matched the performance of leading frontier models at roughly half the cost.

 This compute cost pressure is also emerging in compute markets. 

 The Ornn Compute H100 Price Index, which tracks Nvidia H100 GPU rental prices, surged from ~1.7 in April to a peak of ~3.20 in May before falling sharply to 2.42. 

 This measures the cost of renting AI computing power, primarily used by startups, AI labs, enterprises, and cloud providers to train and run AI models without purchasing GPUs outright. 

 Both token prices and compute rental costs are now retreating from their 2026 highs, suggesting the AI market may be entering a period of normalization after months of explosive demand. 

The key question for the AI industry is whether falling prices generate enough new demand to offset the rapid erosion of pricing power across the industry.

results.title: Accounting Mismatch in AI Profits | Jim Chanos and Val…
highlights:
Speakers see persistent supply constraints and conservative memory producers limiting near‑term capacity, even as empirical AI scaling laws continue to drive compute demand. That mismatch has driven GPU rental spikes, a roughly 40–50% price reversal, and a 4–5x memory surge that markets appear to be mispricing as a near‑term rollover. The panel warns of concentration risk—markets and the U.S. economy are increasingly a bet on AI—while neo‑clouds and leasing layers face low single‑digit ROICs, and semiconductors look constructive but carry bubble risks. They expect a market rotation within 18–24 months that will separate high‑return winners from low‑return, capital‑intensive bets.

...

- Physical supply constraints—equipment vendors can only scale shipments ~30–35% annually and fabs take years and huge capital—help explain the 4–5x surge in DRAM/NAND driven by datacenter AI; speakers expect elevated memory demand to persist for a shallow multi‑year window (roughly 2–4 years), making the market’s pricing that expects a sharp rollover in 6–9 months (forward multiples ~6–7) likely optimistic and shorting DRAM timing‑risky.
- Empirical AI scaling laws (more compute → better models) are driving explosive token usage that is straining GPU capacity and pushing rental prices up roughly 40–50%; Nvidia is deliberately allocating chips across hyperscalers and new cloud/neocloud providers (e.g., CoreWeave) to avoid excessive concentration, effectively routing chips through intermediaries rather than selling only to the largest buyers.
- Neo‑cloud operators function economically like equipment‑leasing/finance firms—buying chips, renting powered rack space and leasing compute—and while tight supply recently improved near‑term economics, current powered‑capacity deals are producing single‑digit pre‑tax ROICs (~5–8%), implying the leasing/middleman layer may offer inferior long‑term returns relative to other stack segments.
- Accounting differences amplify apparent supplier strength: picks‑and‑shovels vendors recognize revenue and profit immediately while hyperscalers capitalize chips, labor and interest for ~12–18 months, mechanically inflating supplier margins even as at least one large model company reported 'absolutely staggering' operating losses in 2025—supporting the view that supplier profitability can diverge from model‑company economics.
- The U.S. economy and equity market are an increasingly concentrated bet on AI—speakers warn of large asymmetric outcomes (huge gains if AI succeeds, large losses if it doesn’t)—and they note historical tech waves (e.g., Netscape/internet era) changed sectoral dynamics without reliably boosting long‑run macro growth, with a market rotation expected to reveal winners and losers within 18–24 months.

...

Supply constraints — Equipment vendors and memory suppliers are cautious and capacity‑constrained. Equipment makers cannot scale shipments much faster than ~30–35% a year, and fabs take years and large capital to build. Memory producers went through a downturn that made management conservative, limiting near‑term capacity growth despite strong demand.

...

## MARKETS

GPU scarcity — Exploding token usage is straining available GPU capacity and pushing rental prices for even older GPUs up. Near‑real‑time token metrics correlate with the rent spike, indicating infrastructure scarcity is driving compute rental inflation.

“These chips are so tight as we speak that the prices rental prices for GPUs which are really old like six, seven, eight years old are going up in price…”— 0:17

Price reversal — GPU rental prices, after a normal year‑over‑year decline into December, tightened sharply since January and jumped roughly 40–50% or more. Newer GPU architectures are more efficient (lower $/token), which should favor replacements, but tight supply changed near‑term economics for neo‑clouds.

“They started to increase by the way into December these prices were down 20 30% year on year which is very normal.”— 13:02

results.title: Daily Investment Brief — June 20, 2026 | Signwl
highlights:
## Market Pulse

The compute market is mid-transition through its most consequential architectural pivot in a decade: training scarcity is giving way to inference scarcity, and the SPOT market is pricing that shift with unusual clarity. Inference-tier GPU SPOT prices are surging across independent markets — A10G up +47.9% in us-ohio over 30 days, L4 up +186% in us-nevada, Inferentia SPOT up +141.7% in de-frankfurt — while on-demand catalog prices for the same and comparable chips (L40S on-demand across all nine regions: exactly 0.0% change over 24h, 7d, and 30d) sit in artificial stasis. That gap between market-clearing SPOT prices and frozen catalog prices is compressed tension, not equilibrium, and the resolution historically moves upward. Compounding the demand signal, the supply side faces structural constraints on two fronts simultaneously: the TSMC/MLCC bottleneck is delaying next-gen Blackwell inference silicon by at least one quarter beyond H2 2026 expectations, and grid interconnection timelines in primary US datacenter corridors have extended to up to 14 years in Northern Virginia. The market is not running out of demand signals — it is running out of places to put capacity.

...

Thesis: Inference-tier GPU SPOT markets in two distinct geographic corridors — the US PJM/Midwest (Ohio, Virginia, Oregon) and Western Europe (Frankfurt, London, Paris) — are experiencing genuine, multi-chip, multi-provider capacity absorption that is not yet reflected in catalog on-demand pricing. This is the most robust signal in the dataset: it repeats across 17 independent A10G SPOT markets, 21 L4 SPOT markets, and is structurally confirmed by the deliberate freeze of L40S on-demand pricing at $1.62/hr across all nine regions. When SPOT markets diverge from on-demand by 15–50% over a single month on hardware with real market depth, the catalog price is lagging the market — not the other way around. The Vultr/HPE GB300 NVL72 deployment (Data Center Knowledge, Jun 17) is the production confirmation: the CEO's description of the shift from "experimentation to customer-facing production" maps directly to the demand-side absorption showing up in SPOT prices. The training→inference transition that analysts have discussed for 18 months is now priced into the spot market.

...

Thesis: Grid interconnection timelines of up to 14 years in Northern Virginia, a 12% utility rate hike in northern Illinois explicitly attributable to AI datacenter load (ComEd, May 2026), Florida SB 484 signed into law prohibiting utilities from passing datacenter costs to residential customers, and NERC's May 2026 formalization of new large-load interconnection protocols have collectively crossed a threshold: energy is no longer an input cost that providers optimize around — it is a supply-side binding constraint analogous to chip fab availability. The geographic price premium visible in us-ohio A10G SPOT ($0.483/hr, +47.9% 30d) relative to se-stockholm ($0.339/hr, +19.9% 30d) and de-frankfurt ($0.357/hr) is, in part, a PJM-territory energy constraint premium being embedded into compute prices in real time. JLL's projection of 100 GW of new datacenter capacity (2026–2030) collides directly with the IEA's estimate that data centers will consume 945 TWh by 2030 — roughly 95% of Japan's current total electricity consumption. The math does not close without structural compute price inflation, geographic diversification, or both. The pricing data already shows both happening simultaneously.

...

Thesis: Hardware that depreciation models say should be decaying at 12.5%/yr is instead being bid up in constrained spot markets — V100_32GB in jp-tokyo is at $1.995/hr, +590% over 30 days, on a chip launched more than eight years ago. This creates a false price floor for legacy inference silicon that will correct violently when Blackwell-class inference capacity becomes widely available. The mechanism is sharp: the generation gap analysis shows that when a successor arrives, the predecessor decays at 77.5%/yr implied rate (L4→L40S transition, just 0.57 years apart). If Blackwell inference (GB300) replays this dynamic against A100 and H100-class inference workloads, the price collapse in legacy silicon will be measured in quarters, not years. However, the stress test revised the timeline materially: MLCC lead times extended from 8 to 20 weeks since April 2026, Murata's Izumo ceramic capacitor facility is at limited capacity until 2027, and Google TPU V8/Trainium4/next-gen NVIDIA production ramps all target H2 2026 but will realistically achieve mass market availability in Q1–Q2 2027. The V100 jp-tokyo anomaly has approximately 9–12 months of shelf life remaining.

...

R4 — MLCC Shortage Extends Blackwell Delay Further The 20-week MLCC lead time reported in June 2026 (DQ, Jun 19) already pushed the Blackwell inference mass-availability estimate to Q1–Q2 2027. If Murata's Izumo facility faces additional production constraints or if additional component shortages emerge in the Blackwell BOM, the delay could push to Q3 2027 — which would extend the legacy silicon price anomaly (H5) but also delay the supply relief for the inference crunch (H1). The risk is asymmetric: extended delays worsen H5's capital allocation problem but are neutral-to-positive for H1's pricing outlook.

results.title: Rising AI Costs Reshape Budgets: Strategies for 2026 Efficiency - AI CERTs News
highlights:
## Why Prices Now Spike

Markets enjoyed a multi-year slide in GPU rental rates until late 2025. In contrast, surging inference demand reversed the curve within six months. Consequently, H100 rates climbed roughly 40%, according to gpu.fund marketplace data. Cast AI added that GPU workloads now consume 40-60% of typical cloud invoices. Moreover, token billing exposes AI budgets to variable spending shocks as usage scales. The result is visible: Rising AI Costs already battered several public company earnings calls. Uber’s technology chief admitted agents burned allocations weeks ahead of plan. Therefore, finance teams monitor every model invocation more closely than marketing impressions.

Hardware optimization can help reduce pressure from rising infrastructure costs.

Rising prices stem from market forces, not isolated vendor greed. However, limited hardware supplies strengthen those forces, leading us to the next challenge.

## Critical Supply Constraints Today

HBM memory capacity remains the tightest choke point in the entire AI stack. Consequently, NVIDIA must ration flagship chips among hyperscalers and specialist clouds. Micron and Samsung plan expansions, yet fabs need years, not quarters. Meanwhile, on-demand cloud prices mirror scarcity signals almost instantly. Marketplace averages jumped from $1.70 to $2.35 per hour within five months. Moreover, some Chinese providers hiked list prices by 400%, shattering previous assumptions. These dynamics amplify Rising AI Costs for global customers lacking reserved capacity. Nevertheless, committed contracts or on-prem deployments can counter volatility when workloads stay predictable.

Supply shortages convert technical bottlenecks into financial pain. Therefore, enterprises must understand budgeting impacts before greenlighting ambitious deployments.

...

Technical and commercial levers can tame unpredictable outlays. Firstly, model distillation shrinks parameters, lowering inference latency and wattage. Secondly, scheduler software shifts workloads to off-peak marketplace slots when possible. Moreover, reserved GPU contracts guarantee capacity at significant discounts for steady demand. Enterprises also recalibrate prompt engineering to trim tokens per interaction. Consequently, these actions directly restrain Rising AI Costs without harming user experience. Additionally, finance teams introduce chargeback models to align enterprise spend with product lines. Teams then benchmark savings against baseline model costs to quantify effectiveness.

results.title: Asia's AI hardware bet has a financing problem - The Business Times
highlights:
THE US cannot sustain its own artificial intelligence boom. Access to power, not capital, is now the biggest bottleneck for new capacity in the country, with new facilities in places such as Virginia waiting as long as seven years for adequate supply.

China, meanwhile, cannot buy Nvidia graphics processing units (GPUs). Washington has restricted AI chip exports since October 2022 and banned every workaround chip that Nvidia designed for the Chinese market. The most recent ban on the Nvidia H20 in April 2025 triggered an announced US$5.5 billion charge for the chipmaker in a single quarter.

South-east Asia’s advantages are clear: open land, available power, and fast permits.

...

The region can build AI data centres, but the tougher question is how to pay for the GPUs inside them. As chips become the dominant cost in AI infrastructure, a new financing market has emerged around the hardware itself – one with its own lenders, risks, and rules.

...

For traditional data centres, IT equipment takes up less than 30 per cent of total capital expenditure. But for AI data centres, GPU servers and related IT equipment account for up to 70 per cent of the total capex.

That shift has turned GPUs into a separate asset class from the data centre facilities that house them. Lenders now finance GPUs separately from the buildings, with different terms and repayment structures.

This new asset class is led by neoclouds, or cloud providers that primarily offer GPU as a service. The neocloud buys GPUs and rents them out by the hour or by the year, copying Amazon Web Services’ playbook without the AWS balance sheet.

To fund the hardware, the neocloud signs an offtake agreement – a multiyear contract in which a customer commits to buy compute capacity in advance. Lenders finance the hardware against that contract, typically placing it in a special purpose vehicle (SPV), a ring-fenced legal entity that holds the assets so the lender can seize them cleanly if payments stop.

...

A major underwriting variable is the schedule. Offtake contracts carry delivery milestones, and the standard remedy for a missed go-live date is the customer’s right to walk away from the contract. Case in point: Microsoft reportedly withdrew from some CoreWeave commitments in early 2025 over delivery issues.

GPUs are ordered months in advance via deposits, so if the chips arrive before the power, they lose value sitting in a warehouse. If the power arrives before the chips, the equity burns on an empty shell.

The transformer order, permits, substation energisation, and GPU procurement all have to land within the same period of time. Otherwise, the customer contract is void.

Investors are also concerned about what makes a project good. As such, South-east Asian neoclouds winning customer contracts today need to deliver on quality, price, and speed.

Quality means Tier III certification, a data centre redundancy standard. Price comes from cheap land and power. Meanwhile, speed is from modular and containerised construction, including prefabricated power and cooling.

The other major issue is residual value, or how much the GPUs will resell for at the end of the term. Equity needs a high residual value to have an attractive return profile on the transaction.

results.title: The AI Supply Chain: Following the $725B (4) - Layer 8 — Cloud (Hyperscaler + Neoclouds)
highlights:
What this layer does

Cloud providers own data centers and chips and rent them by the hour or via long-term contract. Two sub-types: hyperscalers (general-purpose, full-stack, own custom silicon) and neoclouds (GPU-as-a-service pure-plays, faster to spin up GPU capacity).

Who pays whom

Model labs (L9) are the largest customers; enterprises buy AI services on top. Clouds in turn pay L7 (real estate), L6 (networking), L5 (servers), L4 (chips) and L0 (power). Neoclouds raise debt against their hyperscaler/lab contracts to buy GPUs from NVIDIA.

...

Cloud is the toll booth on the whole

...

The revenue-to-capex gap, and what it does to free cash flow. ~$725B of 2026 capex sits against only ~$170B of AI revenue (~4–5× gap), and BofA estimates capex now eats ~94% of operating cash flow after dividends vs a ~40% ten-year norm [10] — increasingly debt- and prepayment-financed. The bull counter is $1.8T+ of contracted backlog, but it’s concentrated in a few labs funded partly by their own suppliers.

Bottleneck - Medium

- Capacity is sold out across AWS/Azure/GCP for 2026 — the constraint is upstream (L4 GPUs, L7 buildings, L0 power), not demand.
- The $725B capex IS the resolution; neoclouds and ex-miners add capacity faster than hyperscalers can build, which is why they exist.
- For neoclouds specifically, the binding constraint is capital and customer concentration: they live or die on a handful of mega-contracts and the debt raised against them.

results.title: Nebius Just Grew Revenue 684%, Now Comes the Hard Part | TIKR.com
highlights:
Eight quarters ago, Nebius was generating $12 million in quarterly revenue. By Q1 2026, that number was $399 million, up 684% year over year and 75% sequentially from Q4 2025. CFO Dado Alonso put it simply on the earnings call: the company sold out its capacity again, because demand continued to exceed available supply. 

That is not a demand problem. That is a capacity problem, and Nebius is spending aggressively to solve it, with capital expenditures of $2.5 billion in Q1 alone and a new 1.2 gigawatt AI factory announced in Pennsylvania. Full-year 2026 revenue guidance sits at $3 to $3.4 billion, supported by over 3 gigawatts of contracted power.

The validation at the top of the market is real and worth taking seriously. NVIDIA has committed to investing $2 billion in Nebius by 2030. When the dominant GPU manufacturer backs one of its customers directly, it signals who gets prioritized when hardware supply is constrained. 

The contracted backlog of approximately $46 billion, anchored by a $27 billion capacity deal with Meta and a $17 billion revenue agreement with Microsoft, provides a foundation that most companies this size could only dream about.

results.title: 박준우 베슬AI 리더 "네오클라우드가 토큰 시대의 해답" < 인터뷰 < AI산업 < 기사본문 - AI타임스
highlights:
지구촌 전체가 극심한 GPU 공급 부족(Shortage) 상태에 빠졌다. 단기간에 공급량을 늘릴 수 없는 구조적 한계 속에서 인프라 시장에는 기존 자원을 아껴 나눠 쓰는 일종의 ‘아나바다’ 바람이 불고 있다.

전 세계에 흩어진 유휴 GPU 자원을 발굴해 실시간 연결하는 네오클라우드 기업 베슬AI의 박준우 GTM(Go-To-Market) 리더를 만나 쇼티지의 현실과 해법을 들었다.

■ 쇼티지보다 무서운 건 확보한 GPU 100% 활용 못 하는 현실

베슬AI는 현재의 쇼티지를 물량 자체가 부족하기도 하지만, 막상 비싼 돈을 들여 칩을 확보하고도 이를 제대로 활용하지 못하는 경우가 허다하다고 진단했다.

박준우 리더는 "엔비디아 블랙웰의 경우 지금 발주를 넣으면 짧게는 6개월, 길게는 1년 이상을 기다려야 한다"라며 "AWS나 GCP 같은 하이퍼스케일러에 의존하자니 최소 3년 약정에 32노드 단위의 대규모 장기 계약이 요구된다"라고 말했다.

이 구조는 단기·소규모 물량이 필요한 대다수 기업의 수요를 수용하지 못하고, 결과적으로 '노는 GPU'를 양산한다. 더욱이 어렵게 확보한 GPU도 하나의 GPU에 모든 작업을 몰아넣다 보니 비효율이 반복된다는 설명이다.

이 지점을 파고든 것이 베슬AI의 ‘네오클라우드’다. 전 세계에 유휴 GPU를 찾아 중개하는 일종의 '에어비앤비' 모델이다.

...

박 리더는 "이 사업의 핵심은 절대적인 GPU 수량이 아니라 고객이 필요한 시점에 그 모델이 있어야 하는 것"이라며 "하이퍼스케일러나 CSP들도 이미 물량을 가동 중이거나 특정 GPU가 부족하면 대응이 안 되는데 그 공백을 채우는 것"이라고 설명했다.

...

최근에는 하이퍼스케일러에서 먼저 문의가 오는 경우가 늘고 있다고 전했다. 하이퍼스케일러는 유휴 자원을 프리 세일즈(Pre-Sales)로 빠르게 처리할 수 있고, 베슬AI는 조기에 많은 물량을 확보할 수 있어 윈-윈(Win-Win) 구조가 형성된다는 것이다.

이는 규모의 경제로 가격 경쟁력을 만든다는 설명이다. 박 리더는 "글로벌 반도체 리서치 전문 세미애널리시스 랭킹 상위권인 GPU 클라우드 기업 대다수와 협업할 만큼 공급사 풀이 많다"라며 "플랫폼 내 거래량이 많아질수록 고객에게 더 합리적인 가격을 제공할 수 있는 구조"라고 설명했다.

실제 북미 시장에서 엔비디아 H100 GPU 기준, 온디맨드 비용을 비교하면 하이퍼스케일러 평균이 시간당 7달러이지만, 베슬AI는 3.28달러로 2배가량 저렴하다.

여기에 분산된 인프라 덕분에 레이턴시(지연) 이슈를 최소화해 신속한 서빙이 가능하며, 보안 거버넌스도 기존 하이퍼스케일러 수준을 상회한다는 평가를 받고 있다.

...

베슬AI는 현재 운용 중인 5000장 규모의 가용 총량을 넘어, 연내 1만장, 차세대 5만 장의 GPU를 확보하여 국내 최대 인프라를 구축할 계획이다.

여기에는 엔비디아의 A100·H100·B300·GB200 뿐만 아니라 구글의 TPU와 국산 NPU 등이 포함돼 있다. '베라 루빈'도 협상 단계다.
